**Memo: Local AI capacity—optimise before we expand**

**To:** Engineering and Finance leadership  
**From:** Platform Engineering  
**Subject:** Whether to buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of the existing fleet

We need to decide whether to buy more local AI hardware or make better use of the fleet we already own. My recommendation is to defer new purchases for one quarter and fund a focused utilisation program, with a pre-approved capital reserve and explicit triggers to buy if the program cannot meet service and throughput targets. This is not a permanent no; it is a sequencing decision that preserves options while we replace assumptions with measurements.

The cost case is less obvious than it appears. Additional accelerators carry purchase price, but also rack space, power, cooling, networking, spares, depreciation, and operational attention. The relevant comparison is not sticker price against zero; it is cost per unit of useful work at the latency we promise. If our current fleet is idle outside business hours, fragmented across small jobs, or blocked by scheduling and model-loading overhead, new hardware will inherit those inefficiencies. Conversely, if we are consistently saturating goodput and queueing delay is rising despite sensible batching, caching, and routing, buying capacity may be cheaper than engineering heroics. We do not yet have a clean enough picture to make that call confidently.

Latency deserves particular care because utilisation programs can go wrong. Packing more work onto the same devices can improve average throughput while making tail latency worse, especially for interactive requests that share pools with batch jobs. We should define service-level objectives by workload class, measure queue time separately from execution time, and reserve headroom for failover and burst. The goal is not maximum utilisation in the abstract; it is high useful utilisation subject to latency and reliability constraints. A system that looks efficient at 95 percent average utilisation but violates p95 latency during routine peaks is not efficient in any business sense.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware adds failure domains, power draw, firmware variance, and operational burden, while a smaller fleet can be simpler to run. But running the existing fleet too hot removes redundancy and makes maintenance risky. The utilisation program should therefore include capacity headroom, drain procedures, and a clear rollback path. We should also track hardware health and error rates, because latent faults can masquerade as capacity shortages.

Opportunity cost is the strongest argument for sequencing. Capital committed to accelerators cannot fund tooling, observability, model optimisation, or reliability work, and engineering time spent tuning schedulers has a cost too. A one-quarter utilisation effort is bounded and reversible: if it succeeds, we avoid or defer capital expense; if it fails, we will have better evidence for the purchase and a cleaner specification for what to buy. Hardware procurement is much less reversible. Lead times, depreciation, and integration work make an early purchase expensive to undo, and the accelerator market may look different in six months.

I acknowledge real uncertainty. Workload forecasts are noisy, our utilisation telemetry is incomplete, and some latency-sensitive workloads may genuinely need dedicated capacity. That is why I recommend a gated approach rather than an open-ended optimisation project. Set a budget and a deadline, define the metrics that matter—goodput per accelerator, queue delay by class, batch efficiency, idle and fragmentation rates, and incident impact—and pre-commit to buying if we cannot meet agreed targets without violating latency or reliability objectives. Keep a small reserve for spares and urgent demand, but do not expand the fleet on the assumption that demand will arrive.

In short, improve utilisation first, but do so with discipline and a credible exit. We should treat new hardware as the right answer only when measured demand, not discomfort, justifies it. If the utilisation program clears the agreed gates, we buy with better information and less regret. If it does not, we will have bought time, learned where the real bottleneck is, and preserved the option to spend later.

**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Engineering Leadership  
**From:** Platform Engineering  
**Subject:** Local AI capacity: improve utilisation before buying more hardware

We need to decide whether to add local AI hardware or to get more useful capacity out of the equipment we already own. The instinct to buy is understandable: demand is growing, queues are visible, and new GPUs are the most direct answer. But the stronger near-term recommendation is to improve utilisation first, with a time-boxed effort and explicit purchase triggers. We should not treat additional hardware as the default response until we have measured where our current capacity is actually going and whether the bottleneck is compute, memory, scheduling, model choice, or operational headroom.

The cost case is broader than the purchase price. Additional local AI hardware brings power, cooling, rack space, support, spare parts, and integration work, and it consumes the scarcest resource this team has: engineering attention. A small team can absorb one more node far more easily than it can absorb a new capacity-planning and failure-handling regime. Idle or poorly scheduled hardware is expensive even when it looks cheap on a quote. Utilisation work also has a cost, because tuning schedulers, batching, caching, model routing, and admission control takes time, but that work is usually smaller, can be staged, and leaves us with better operational knowledge regardless of whether we eventually buy.

Latency and reliability cut both ways. Better packing can reduce queueing and improve throughput, but aggressive batching or overcommitment can damage tail latency and make failure modes worse. Utilisation is not simply a matter of driving average GPU usage higher; we need to track goodput, p95 queue wait, latency SLO attainment, memory pressure, and the blast radius of a single node failure. More hardware can improve reliability through redundancy, but it also adds another system to patch, monitor, and debug. If our real problem is the absence of N+1 headroom for a latency-sensitive service, a targeted redundancy purchase may be justified even when average utilisation is modest. That is a reliability decision, not a capacity decision, and we should name it as such.

Opportunity cost and reversibility point in the same direction. Capital spent on hardware is difficult to unwind, and the architecture we build around it can become sticky. Software and scheduling changes are comparatively reversible; if a tuning experiment fails, we can roll it back. A short-term rented or cloud burst can also act as a reversible bridge where data and security constraints permit, though it is not a substitute for a durable local strategy. The opportunity cost of a utilisation sprint is real: it delays feature work and may not produce the gains we hope for. That is why the effort should be capped and judged against pre-agreed metrics rather than allowed to become an open-ended optimisation project.

My recommendation is therefore to defer additional local AI hardware for this budget cycle and run a focused six-to-eight-week utilisation program. It should measure demand by model and tenant, identify the actual constraint, and implement the highest-leverage changes with guardrails for tail latency and reliability. We should authorise a purchase only if the data shows sustained demand exceeding usable capacity after optimisation, or if a specific reliability gap requires redundancy. We should also be honest about uncertainty: workload forecasts are noisy, optimisation gains are not guaranteed, and vendor lead times may force an earlier decision than we would like. The answer is not to pretend we know the future, but to choose the reversible step first and set a review date with clear thresholds. If those thresholds are crossed, we buy deliberately rather than reactively.

Internal Engineering Memo

Subject: Local AI capacity—buy more hardware or improve utilisation?

The immediate question is whether to add local AI hardware or to get more useful work from the equipment we already own. My recommendation is to defer additional hardware for one quarter and run a focused utilisation program, with a pre-agreed trigger for incremental purchase if measured demand proves we are genuinely constrained. This is not an argument that hardware is unimportant. It is an argument that capital should follow evidence, and we do not yet have enough evidence that compute capacity, rather than scheduling and operational practice, is the binding constraint.

Cost is the first reason for caution. The purchase price of additional accelerators is only part of the bill; servers, networking, storage, power, cooling, rack space, spares, depreciation, and the engineering time to operate a larger fleet all compound it. A utilisation program also costs money, principally in scarce engineering attention, so the comparison is not free software against expensive hardware. The right metric is cost per useful inference or token under our latency and reliability objectives, not nominal GPU-hours or headline utilisation. If capacity is being lost to fragmented reservations, poor batching, oversized models, duplicate caches, or idle tenants, we can recover meaningful headroom for a fraction of a hardware purchase. If the remaining waste is small, that finding is itself valuable: it tells us to buy.

Latency complicates the picture because more hardware can reduce queueing and tail latency, while aggressive utilisation can harm it. Batching, oversubscription, and consolidation improve throughput but can increase p95 and p99 response times. We should therefore optimise against explicit service-level objectives, separating interactive and batch work, using priority queues, admission control, preemption, caching, quantization, and model routing where they preserve the user experience. If, after safe optimisation, peak p95 queueing still breaches our objectives and we lack failover headroom, that is a strong signal to add capacity. If we meet the objectives with room to spare, buying more would mainly increase idle inventory.

Reliability cuts both ways. A larger fleet adds failure domains, driver and firmware complexity, power and cooling risk, and operational burden for a small team. Consolidation can improve efficiency but may reduce redundancy, so utilisation targets must not approach one hundred percent; we need reserved headroom for failures, bursts, and maintenance. Low utilisation may also be hiding weak observability or fragile scheduling. Buying more hardware can mask those problems rather than solve them. Conversely, if a single node failure predictably breaches our objectives, redundancy is a legitimate reason to add capacity, though scheduling and spare capacity should be evaluated first.

Opportunity cost and reversibility are decisive. Capital committed to hardware is lumpy, depreciates, and is difficult to reverse, especially with long lead times and uncertain vendor roadmaps. Model architectures, quantization, and serving efficiency are changing quickly, so the shape of capacity we need in six months may differ from today’s. Software and scheduling improvements are comparatively reversible: we can tune them, roll them back, and learn from them. A short-term cloud burst or lease can bridge uncertain peaks where data residency, egress, and latency permit, preserving options while we measure.

I recommend a six-to-eight-week utilisation program that instruments per-GPU and per-tenant utilisation, memory pressure, queue delay, cache efficiency, and failure headroom; implements SLO-aware scheduling, quotas, batching, and model placement; and establishes cost per inference. We should commit in advance to purchase triggers: sustained peak utilisation above roughly seventy to seventy-five percent after optimisation, repeated p95 queue-latency breaches, inability to maintain failover headroom, or a credible growth forecast that exceeds those limits. If a trigger fires, buy incrementally rather than in one large commitment, and keep a lease or cloud-burst option available. The uncertainty is real: demand may spike, model mix may shift, and software gains may be smaller than expected. Revisit the decision quarterly. On current evidence, improve utilisation first and buy only against a measured, sustained shortfall.

MEMORANDUM  
To: Engineering Leadership  
From: Platform Engineering  
Date: [date]  
Subject: Local AI capacity: improve utilisation before buying more hardware

We need to choose between buying additional local AI hardware and getting more useful capacity out of the equipment we already own. The question is not whether additional hardware would help; it is whether the next unit of capacity is better bought or recovered from the equipment we have. My recommendation is to improve utilisation first, but to do so as a bounded, instrumented program with explicit purchase triggers rather than as an open-ended optimisation exercise. We should not treat “buy” and “optimise” as permanent camps. The right answer depends on measured demand, latency sensitivity, and the operational cost of running closer to the edge. At present, we do not have enough evidence to justify a capital purchase, and the software and scheduling changes available to us are more reversible.

The cost case is broader than the purchase price. Additional accelerators bring power, cooling, rack space, support contracts, spare parts, and depreciation, and they consume scarce engineering attention. A small team can easily spend more on integration and operations than it saves by avoiding a hardware order. Conversely, utilisation work is not free: instrumentation, scheduling, batching, model routing, caching, and quota enforcement all take time, and that time has an opportunity cost against product work. The program should therefore be time-boxed and judged against a simple threshold: if the engineering effort to recover capacity costs more than the capacity is worth, we should buy or rent instead. We should also compare against cloud burst or leasing, which can bridge a peak without committing capital.

Latency and reliability are the constraints that matter most. Average utilisation is a poor guide; a cluster at 60 percent average can still have painful p95 and p99 queueing at peak, and a cluster at 90 percent can be stable if workloads are predictable and isolated. We need per-workload demand, queue time, memory pressure, preemption, failure, and retry data before we decide. Better scheduling, fair quotas, batching where latency budgets allow, and routing small requests to smaller models can recover real capacity and sometimes improve tail latency by preventing one workload from starving another. But optimisation has limits. Running with no headroom makes failover, maintenance, and bursts fragile, and aggressive batching can hurt interactive latency. More hardware reduces queueing and adds redundancy, but it also adds failure domains and operational burden. If we are missing latency objectives at peak after safe optimisation, or if a single node failure threatens service, that is a reliability argument for capacity, not a utilisation argument.

Reversibility should tilt the initial decision. Scheduling policies, quotas, caches, and routing rules can be changed or rolled back in days. Hardware purchases depreciate, may be hard to resell, and can lock us into a vendor or architecture just before the roadmap shifts. Delay is not free, however: persistent latency problems and slow experiments have a real opportunity cost, and waiting for perfect data can be as expensive as buying too early. The practical answer is a staged commitment. I recommend an eight-to-twelve-week utilisation program with clear owners, dashboards, and a review date. We should pre-agree the triggers for purchase: sustained peak utilisation above a safe operating threshold, repeated misses of latency objectives despite optimisation, forecast demand that exceeds recoverable capacity, or a cost-per-request comparison that favours new hardware. If those triggers are met, we buy without reopening the whole debate. If they are not, we extend the program only if it is still yielding measurable capacity.

There is genuine uncertainty here. Demand forecasts are noisy, optimisation gains are hard to predict, and hardware roadmaps can change quickly. That argues for keeping the decision reversible and for measuring before committing. My recommendation is therefore to improve utilisation first under a capped program, use cloud or leasing as a temporary bridge if needed, and hold a standing option to buy more local hardware once the triggers are met. This gives us the cost discipline of optimisation without pretending that software can always substitute for capacity.

**Internal Engineering Memo**

To: AI Platform Steering Group  
From: Platform Engineering  
Subject: Local AI capacity: buy more hardware or improve utilisation?

The capacity question has arrived as a binary choice, but it is not one. We can buy more local AI hardware, or we can make better use of the hardware we already own, and in practice the right answer is a sequenced combination. My recommendation is to fund a focused utilisation program first, with a small reversible buffer and explicit purchase triggers, rather than committing to a broad hardware expansion now. The case for buying is real, but it should be earned by evidence that demand exceeds what disciplined operation can deliver.

Cost is the first reason for caution. The purchase price of a node is only the visible part; depreciation, power, cooling, rack space, support, spares, and the engineering time to operate it all compound. For a small team, every additional node is also an additional failure domain, upgrade path, and on-call surface. Utilisation work is not free either, because it consumes scarce engineering attention and can introduce latency trade-offs, but it is usually cheaper and more incremental than capex. The relevant metric is not raw GPU-hours but cost per useful unit of work: a well-scheduled, right-sized fleet at moderate utilisation can beat an underused larger fleet on total cost.

Latency and reliability cut both ways. More hardware can reduce contention, shorten queues, and isolate latency-critical workloads, which is exactly what we want when service-level objectives are at risk. But if low utilisation comes from fragmentation, idle reservations, oversized models, or poor scheduling, adding hardware simply reproduces the inefficiency at greater cost. Conversely, utilisation improvements such as admission control, quotas, caching, right-sizing, and latency-aware batching can improve reliability and tail latency, provided we do not overcommit or batch so aggressively that interactive work suffers. We need observability that distinguishes genuine capacity shortage from queueing caused by policy, and guardrails that protect p95 latency and error budgets.

Opportunity cost and reversibility should shape the sequence. Capital committed to hardware is difficult to unwind, depreciates on a fixed schedule, and can lock us into a vendor or architecture just as model efficiency and workload mix are changing quickly. Utilisation improvements are largely reversible: we can tune scheduling, reclaim idle reservations, adjust quotas, and roll back changes that hurt latency. A lease or cloud burst is also a useful reversible bridge for peak demand, though it carries its own cost and data-governance constraints. Delaying all hardware purchase indefinitely is not free either, because persistent queueing erodes developer productivity and can breach commitments. The decision should therefore be time-boxed and measured.

My concrete recommendation is a six-to-eight week utilisation sprint with a pre-agreed review. The team should instrument per-workload utilisation, queue wait, p95 latency, error rates, and idle reasons; then reclaim idle capacity, tighten scheduling and quotas, right-size models, apply quantization or caching where quality allows, and evaluate partitioning or power caps. We should set purchase triggers in advance. If, after those changes, peak sustained utilisation remains high, queue delays breach service objectives, and forecast demand exceeds capacity for two consecutive quarters, we should buy incrementally rather than in a large block. A single-node expansion, a lease, or a cloud burst should be tried before a major commitment. If a workload genuinely requires isolation or hard latency guarantees, dedicated hardware may be justified even at lower utilisation, because reliability has value that utilisation percentages do not capture.

The uncertainty is genuine. Demand forecasts are noisy, model efficiency can improve faster than expected, and our own utilisation data is currently too coarse to support a large purchase. The thresholds above are provisional and should be revised at the review. What is not uncertain is the direction: improve utilisation first, keep the bridge reversible, and let measured shortfalls trigger hardware purchases. That approach protects cost, latency, and reliability while preserving the option to expand when the evidence is strong.
